lessons.notes_html:
Three Main Parts

A seed has three main parts. The seed coat covers the seed from outside and protects it. The cotyledons are inside the seed and food is stored in them. The embryo is the tiny young plant inside the seed.

Work of Each Part

Food stored in the cotyledons feeds the new plant at the time of germination. Maize and wheat have one cotyledon, while bean and gram have two cotyledons. The upper part of the embryo is called the plumule and it makes the shoot and leaves. The lower part is called the radicle and it makes the root.

Key Points

  • Cotyledons store food for germination.

lessons.title: Germination and Its Conditions
lessons.notes_html:
What Germination Needs

Germination is the start of growth of a seed. Three things are necessary for germination: water, air and suitable warmth. Germination stops if any one of these conditions is missing.

Work of Water, Air and Warmth

Water makes the seed soft and the young plant inside starts growing. Air means oxygen, which is needed by the seed for breathing and getting energy. A seed germinates quickly in suitable warmth. In too much cold or too much heat, it cannot germinate.

Steps of Germination

  • The seed absorbs water and becomes soft.
  • The seed coat breaks.
  • The root comes out downwards.
  • The shoot and leaves come out upwards.

Key Points

  • Water, air and suitable warmth are all needed.
  • Water softens the seed so growth can start.
  • Oxygen in air gives energy for breathing.
  • Root grows downwards and shoot grows upwards.

lessons.notes_html:
Meaning of Pollution

When the air, water or land around us becomes dirty and harmful, it is called pollution. The thing or substance which causes pollution is called a pollutant. Examples of pollutants are smoke, sewage water, chemicals and plastic. Pollution is harmful for human beings, animals and plants alike.

Four Types of Pollution

  • Air pollution
  • Water pollution
  • Land pollution, also called soil pollution
  • Noise pollution

Why Smoke Is Harmful

Smoke contains harmful gases and tiny particles of dust. When we breathe air full of smoke, these enter our lungs and cause cough, breathing problems and diseases like asthma. Smoke makes it difficult to see and forms a layer on the leaves of plants, which stops their growth.

Key Points

  • A pollutant is the substance that causes pollution.

lessons.title: Keeping Air and Water Clean
lessons.notes_html:
Do Not Burn Crop Remains

Farmers should not burn the remains of crops. Burning produces a lot of smoke, which pollutes the air and makes people sick. The fire also kills the useful insects and microorganisms of the soil and reduces the fertility of the soil. Instead, the remains should be mixed in the soil so they rot and become natural manure, which is useful for the crop.

How Trees Clean the Air

Trees absorb carbon dioxide from the air and give out oxygen, which keeps the air clean and fresh. The leaves of trees stop the dust and smoke of the air and give shade and coolness in summer. More trees mean less air pollution, so we should plant more and more trees.

Protecting Water

  • Do not throw dirt, garbage and sewage into rivers, canals and wells.
  • Factories must not release chemical water into water without cleaning it.
  • Do not wash clothes and animals near sources of drinking water.
  • Keep cleanliness around hand pumps and wells.

Key Points

  • Mix crop remains in soil to make natural manure.
  • Burning remains kills useful soil insects and microorganisms.
  • Trees absorb carbon dioxide and give out oxygen.
  • Keep garbage, sewage and chemical water out of rivers and wells.

How Germs Reach Drinking Water

Germs mix in water along with dirt. If open wells and hand pumps are near a dirty drain, dirty water seeps into the water. Rain water washes dirt into ponds and rivers. Germs also reach water through dirty hands and dirty pots. Drinking such polluted water causes diseases like cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea.

Noise Pollution

Sources of noise pollution are horns of vehicles, loud sound of loudspeakers, noise of factories and generators, sound of aeroplanes and construction work. Too much noise reduces hearing power and causes headache and lack of sleep. Students cannot concentrate on their studies and people remain irritable and sick.

Cutting Trees Harms Animals

Trees are the homes of animals and birds and a source of their food. By cutting trees, birds lose their nests and animals lose their shelter. Many animals die due to lack of food or move to other places, and some kinds of animals are finished forever. Cutting trees also increases soil erosion and disturbs the whole food chain.

Key Points

  • Germs reach water from dirty drains, rain-washed dirt and dirty hands and pots.
  • Polluted water causes cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea.
  • Noise harms hearing, sleep and study concentration.
  • Cutting trees takes away nests, shelter and food of animals.

lessons.notes_html:
Three States of Matter

Matter is found in three states: solid, liquid and gas. Ice is a solid, water is a liquid and steam is a gas. Each state behaves in its own way because its particles are arranged differently.

Particles in Gases

In gases, the particles of matter move freely in all directions. In a solid such as ice, the particles stay in fixed positions. When ice gets heat, its particles start moving more, leave their fixed positions and begin to flow.

Key Points

  • Matter has three states: solid, liquid and gas.
  • Gas particles move freely in all directions.
  • On heating, a solid changes to liquid and then to gas.
  • The order of change is melting and then evaporation.

lessons.notes_html:
Melting and Freezing

Melting is the process in which a solid changes into a liquid on heating, for example ice changing into water. It happens at a fixed temperature called the melting point. Ice melts at 0°C. Freezing is the opposite process, in which a liquid changes into a solid on cooling. Water freezes into ice at 0°C.

What Happens to an Ice Cube

An ice cube absorbs heat from the surrounding air and slowly melts into water. Until the ice melts completely, its temperature stays at 0°C, although its mass remains the same. In the cooling curve of ice formation, the flat part parallel to the time axis shows water changing into ice at a constant 0°C. To carry ice home without melting, wrap it in thick cloth, newspaper or sawdust, keep it in a thermos or closed box away from sunlight, and buy one big piece because it melts more slowly.

Key Points

  • Melting is solid to liquid on heating at a fixed melting point.
  • Ice melts at 0°C and water freezes at 0°C.
  • While ice melts, its temperature stays at 0°C.
  • Thick cloth, newspaper or a thermos slows down melting.
  • One big piece of ice melts more slowly than small pieces.

lessons.notes_html:
Evaporation and Boiling

Evaporation is the change of a liquid into a gas. When a solid is heated, it first melts into a liquid and then changes into a gas by evaporation. Water boils at 100°C.

Sublimation and Cooling

Camphor is an example of sublimation. We feel cooling near an ice-cream cart because melting ice absorbs heat from its surroundings, and salt mixed with the ice keeps the ice cream frozen. An ice lolly melts faster in a warm place and slowly in a cool place, and its temperature stays the same while it is melting.

Key Points

  • Evaporation changes a liquid into a gas.
  • Water boils at 100°C.
  • Camphor is an example of sublimation.
  • Melting ice absorbs heat, so the air near an ice-cream cart feels cool.
  • An ice lolly melts faster in a warm place.

lessons.notes_html:
Parts of a Lever

A lever is a rigid bar or plank which can turn around a fixed point and helps in lifting a load. The fulcrum is the fixed point on which the lever rests and turns. The load is the heavy object to be lifted or moved. The effort is the force applied by us to lift the load. So the statement that load is the point where a lever is supported is false; that point is the fulcrum.

Three Kinds of Lever

  • First kind: the fulcrum in the middle.
  • Second kind: the load in the middle, as in a wheelbarrow and a nail cutter.
  • Third kind: the effort in the middle, as in tongs.

Key Points

  • A lever turns around a fixed point called the fulcrum.
  • Load is the heavy object and effort is the force we apply.
  • First kind has the fulcrum in the middle.
  • Second kind has the load in the middle, like a wheelbarrow.
  • Third kind has the effort in the middle, like tongs.

lessons.notes_html:

A pulley is a small wheel with a groove around its rim. A rope passes over it, which makes lifting a load easier and changes the direction of force. A pulley is used to draw water from a well.

An inclined plane helps us push a heavy load up and also take it down safely with less force. Machines make work easier by reducing the force, but they do not reduce the total work done, because the load has to travel a longer distance.

Key Points

  • A pulley is a small wheel with a groove and a rope over it.
  • A pulley lifts a load and changes the direction of force.
  • An inclined plane helps to push a load up and take it down.
  • Machines reduce force but do not reduce total work.

lessons.notes_html:
Light Falls on Objects

We see a thing when light from a source of light, such as the Sun or a bulb, falls on it. The light then reflects from the object into our eyes. When this reflected light reaches our eyes, we can see the object.

Why Some Things Cannot Be Seen

In a dark room there is no light, so no rays reflect from the objects and no light reaches our eyes. That is why nothing is visible in the dark. As soon as a lamp is lit, the objects become visible. We also cannot see the particles of air because they are very small and transparent. Light hardly reflects from them, so they cannot be seen. The wall of a room is solid and a lot of light reflects from it, so it is clearly visible.

Transparent Materials and Straight Lines

  • Transparent materials allow light to pass through them.
  • Clear glass is a transparent material.
  • Light travels in a straight line.

Key Points

  • Light from a source falls on objects and reflects into our eyes.
  • Nothing is visible in a dark room because no light reflects.
  • Air particles are too small and transparent to be seen.
  • Transparent materials let light pass through them.
  • Light travels in a straight line.

lessons.notes_html:
How a Shadow Forms

A shadow forms when an object blocks the path of light. Light travels in a straight line, so it cannot pass through the object. The dark part behind the object, where the light cannot reach, is its shadow.

Big and Small Shadows

When an object is near a source of light, it blocks more rays of light, so its shadow is formed bigger. As the object goes away from the source, it blocks fewer rays and the shadow becomes smaller. It is not true that only big objects make shadows. Small objects also block light and make shadows.

Shadows Tell the Time

  • The Sun changes its place during the day, so shadows change too.
  • By noting the length of the shadow we can tell the time of day.

Key Points

  • A shadow forms when an object blocks light.
  • Near the light source, the shadow is bigger.
  • Far from the light source, the shadow is smaller.
  • Not only big objects make shadows.
  • The length of a shadow can tell the time of day.

lessons.notes_html:
Sunlight Has Seven Colours

White sunlight is a mixture of seven colours. When sunlight passes through a prism, it bends and splits into seven different colours. This band of colours is called a spectrum.

  • Red
  • Orange
  • Yellow
  • Green
  • Sky blue
  • Indigo, also called deep blue
  • Violet

Why a Shirt Looks Black

A black surface absorbs all the colours of light and reflects no colour back. When no light reflects from the shirt into our eyes, it appears black to us.

The Rainbow

When sunlight passes through the tiny drops of rain, it bends and splits into seven colours. Countless drops in the sky split the light in this way, so a rainbow always appears in the shape of a big coloured arc. A rainbow has seven colours, not ten.

Key Points

  • Sunlight is a mixture of seven colours.
  • A prism splits sunlight into a spectrum.
  • A black shirt absorbs all colours and reflects none.

lessons.notes_html:
Electricity Made by Friction

Static electricity is produced by friction, that is, by rubbing two things together. This electricity stays at one place and does not flow like the current in wires.

Two Examples

  • Rubbing a plastic comb in dry hair produces static electricity, and the comb attracts small pieces of paper.
  • Rubbing a balloon on hair or a woollen cloth produces electricity in it, and the balloon sticks to the wall.
  • Hair can also be electrified by friction.

Charges

Objects that carry the same kind of charge push each other away. Like charges repel each other. The current that flows in the wires of our homes is not static electricity, because static electricity stays at one place.

Key Points

  • Static electricity is produced by friction.
  • It stays at one place and does not flow.
  • A rubbed comb attracts small pieces of paper.
  • A rubbed balloon sticks to the wall.
  • Like charges repel each other.

lessons.notes_html:
Open Circuit

An open circuit is a circuit in which the path of electricity is broken somewhere. In an open circuit, current does not flow and the bulb does not glow.

Closed Circuit

A closed circuit is a circuit in which the path is complete and unbroken. In a closed circuit, current flows and the bulb glows. Opening and closing a switch makes the circuit open and closed.

Parts of a Simple Circuit

  • A cell or battery, the source of electricity
  • Wires, the path of electricity
  • A bulb, which uses electricity
  • A switch, to open and close the circuit

When the switch is closed, current comes out of the cell, reaches the bulb through the wires and returns to the cell, so the bulb glows. If both wires are joined to the same terminal of the cell, or a wire is disconnected, the bulb does not glow.

Key Points

  • Open circuit: the path is broken, current does not flow, the bulb does not glow.
  • Closed circuit: the path is complete, current flows, the bulb glows.
  • A switch opens and closes the circuit.
  • A simple circuit has four parts: cell, wires, bulb and switch.

Electromagnets

An electromagnet can be made with wire wound around an iron nail and connected to electricity. The wire forms turns, also called coils, around the nail.

Making It Stronger

The flow of current in an electromagnet can be increased by increasing the number of turns of wire around the iron nail. More turns of wire means a stronger flow of current in the electromagnet.

The Compass

Key Points

  • More turns of wire increase the flow of current in an electromagnet.

Types and Components of Soil
lessons.notes_html:
Types of Soil

There are three main types of soil. Sandy soil has big particles. Clayey soil has very fine particles. Loam is a complete type of soil made by mixing sand, clay and humus.

A clay pot is not a type of soil. It is a thing made from soil. Garden soil, sandy soil and clayey soil are real types of soil.

Four Components of Soil

Soil has four main components:

  • Mineral particles: sand, silt and clay, formed by the breaking of rocks.
  • Humus: the matter of decayed plants and animals, which gives food to the soil.
  • Water: it stays between the particles of soil and is available to plants.
  • Air: it stays in the spaces between the particles and is necessary for roots and small organisms.

An earthworm is a living thing, while soil, water and sunlight are non-living things.

Key Points

  • The three soil types are sandy soil, clayey soil and loam.
  • Soil has four components: mineral particles, humus, water and air.
  • Humus is made of decayed plants and animals.
  • A clay pot is made from soil; it is not a soil type.

lessons.title: Layers of Soil and Percolation
lessons.notes_html:
The Jar Experiment

Take soil up to half in a glass jar, fill it with water and shake it well. Then keep it still for a few hours. The heavy and big particles of sand settle at the very bottom. Above the sand comes silt, and above it the fine clay. Decayed leaves and humus keep floating on the water at the top. This shows that soil is a mixture of particles of different sizes.

Percolation

When water is poured on dry soil, the water goes down through the small spaces between the particles and the soil becomes wet. This process of water passing down through the soil is called percolation.

Water percolates quickly through sandy soil, while this process is very slow in clayey soil.

Sticky and Non-Sticky Soils

Sandy soil is non-sticky. Its particles are big and water drains away quickly, so it does not stick to the hands. Clayey soil has very fine particles; it holds water and becomes soft and sticky.

Key Points

  • In the jar experiment, sand settles at the bottom and humus floats on top.
  • Percolation is water passing down through the spaces between soil particles.
  • Water percolates fast in sandy soil and very slowly in clayey soil.
  • Sandy soil is non-sticky; clayey soil is sticky and holds water.

mcqs.why: Sand particles are heavy and big, so in the jar experiment they settle at the very bottom.

mcqs.q: In the jar experiment, what floats on top of the water?
mcqs.why: Decayed leaves and humus are light, so they keep floating on the water at the top of the jar.

mcqs.why: Percolation is the process of water passing down through the small spaces between soil particles.

lessons.title: Soil and Plant Growth
lessons.notes_html:
Loam: The Best Soil for Plants

Soil type 4, which is loam, a mixture of all the three soils, is the best for the growth of plants. It is a balanced mixture of sand, clay and humus.

  • Sand manages air and drainage of water in the soil.
  • Clay holds water in the soil.
  • Humus gives food to the plants.

Because of this balance, roots grow easily and plants grow healthy and fast in loam.

Dead Organic Matter

Dead organic matter comes from things that were once living, such as a dead ant, a banana peel and a fallen leaf. Such matter mixes in the soil and helps it. A plastic bag does not make soil fertile.

Watering Plants

When you water the plants, not all the water is absorbed. Some water drains down through the soil, so the statement that all the water is absorbed is false.

Key Points

  • Loam, soil type 4, is the best soil for plant growth.
  • Sand manages air and drainage, clay holds water, humus gives food.
  • Dead ant, banana peel and fallen leaf are dead organic matter.
  • Plastic does not make soil fertile.
  • Not all water poured on plants is absorbed by them.

lessons.title: The Sun and the Planets
lessons.notes_html:
The Eight Planets

Our solar system has eight planets. In order from the Sun they are: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

How Planets Move

Planets move around the Sun in elliptical orbits. The Moon is not a planet or a star; it is a satellite of the Earth.

Smallest and Largest

Mercury is the smallest planet, and it is also the closest planet to the Sun. Jupiter is the largest planet of the solar system.

Key Points

  • There are eight planets, from Mercury nearest the Sun to Neptune farthest.
  • Planets move around the Sun in elliptical orbits.
  • The Moon is a satellite of the Earth.
  • Mercury is the smallest planet; Jupiter is the largest.

mcqs.q: How many planets are there in our solar system?
mcqs.why: Our solar system has eight planets, from Mercury nearest the Sun to Neptune farthest from it.

mcqs.q: Which planet is nearest to the Sun?
mcqs.why: Mercury is the first planet from the Sun, so it is the closest planet to the Sun.

mcqs.q: Planets move around the Sun in:
mcqs.why: Planets move around the Sun in elliptical orbits, not in circular or other shaped paths.

mcqs.why: The Moon is a satellite of the Earth because it moves around the Earth.

mcqs.q: Which is the smallest planet?
mcqs.why: Mercury is the smallest planet of the solar system, smaller than Mars, Venus and Earth.

mcqs.q: Which is the largest planet?
mcqs.why: Jupiter is the largest planet, bigger than Saturn, Earth and Neptune.

mcqs.q: Which planet comes third from the Sun?
mcqs.why: The order from the Sun is Mercury, Venus and then Earth, so Earth is third from the Sun.

mcqs.q: Which planet is farthest from the Sun?
mcqs.why: Neptune is the eighth planet, so it is the farthest planet from the Sun.

mcqs.q: Which planet comes just after Mars in order from the Sun?
mcqs.why: The order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars and then Jupiter, so Jupiter comes just after Mars.

mcqs.why: Mercury is both the smallest planet and the closest planet to the Sun.

lessons.title: Special Features of the Planets
lessons.notes_html:
Venus and Mars

Venus is called the morning star. It is the hottest planet because its thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide works like a blanket: it lets the heat of the Sun come in but does not let it go out. This is called the greenhouse effect. So Venus is hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

Mars is the red planet. It has a thin atmosphere and the largest volcano of the solar system, Olympus Mons.

Earth and Jupiter

The atmosphere of Earth is mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Earth has liquid water on its surface and life exists on it. It is the third planet from the Sun and has only one moon.

Jupiter is the biggest planet. Its atmosphere is hydrogen and helium, it has a Great Red Spot, and its moon Ganymede is the biggest moon.

Saturn and Neptune

Saturn appears yellowish. It has the most moons, 82 in total, and its rings are made of ice and dust particles.

Neptune is the coldest planet. It is deep blue in colour, eighth from the Sun, has six rings, and takes about 165 years to revolve around the Sun.

Key Points

  • Venus is the morning star and the hottest planet, due to the greenhouse effect.
  • Mars is the red planet with the largest volcano, Olympus Mons.
  • Saturn has the most moons, 82, and rings of ice and dust.
  • Neptune is the coldest planet, with six rings and about 165 years per revolution.

mcqs.why: Venus shines brightly in the morning sky, so it is known as the morning star.

mcqs.q: Which is the hottest planet?
mcqs.why: Venus is the hottest planet because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps the heat of the Sun.

It has no atmosphere at all
mcqs.why: The thick carbon dioxide atmosphere of Venus works like a blanket and traps heat, which is the greenhouse effect.

mcqs.why: Mars, the red planet, has the largest volcano of the solar system, called Olympus Mons.

mcqs.why: Earth is the planet whose atmosphere is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with liquid water and life on it.

mcqs.why: Ganymede, a moon of Jupiter, is the biggest moon; Jupiter also has the Great Red Spot.

mcqs.why: Saturn has the most moons, 82 in total, more than Jupiter, Uranus or Earth.

mcqs.q: Which is the coldest planet?
mcqs.why: Neptune, the farthest and deep blue planet, is the coldest planet of the solar system.

mcqs.why: According to the book, Neptune has six rings, and it is the eighth planet from the Sun.

mcqs.why: Neptune is very far from the Sun, so it takes about 165 years to complete one revolution.

lessons.title: Moons, Dwarf Planets and Space Objects
lessons.notes_html:
Moons of the Planets

Mercury has no moon at all, and Venus also has no moon. Earth has one moon, and Mars has two moons. Saturn has the most moons, 82 in total.

Dwarf Planets

Pluto is a dwarf planet. It is much smaller than the eight main planets, so it is not counted among them.

Asteroids and Comets

Asteroids are small rocky pieces which revolve around the Sun. Most of them are found between Mars and Jupiter. A comet is a ball of ice, dust and rock. When a comet comes near the Sun, its ice melts and forms a long shining tail.

Studying Space

A telescope is an instrument with which distant objects appear big and clear. Astronomers study the Moon, planets, stars and other objects in space with a telescope.

Key Points

  • Mercury and Venus have no moons; Earth has one and Mars has two.
  • Pluto is a dwarf planet.
  • Asteroids are small rocky pieces, mostly between Mars and Jupiter.
  • Comets are balls of ice, dust and rock that grow a shining tail near the Sun.
  • A telescope makes distant objects appear big and clear.

mcqs.why: Mercury has no moon at all; Venus also has no moon, while Earth has one and Mars has two.

mcqs.q: Which planet has exactly two moons?
mcqs.why: Mars has two moons, while Earth has one and Mercury and Venus have none.

mcqs.why: Pluto is a dwarf planet, while Neptune, Mercury and Earth are among the eight main planets.

mcqs.why: Asteroids are small rocky pieces which revolve around the Sun, mostly between Mars and Jupiter.

mcqs.why: Most asteroids are found in the region between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

mcqs.why: A comet is a ball of ice, dust and rock, unlike an asteroid which is made of rock.

It makes sound from space louder
It makes distant objects appear big and clear

mcqs.why: Mercury and Venus are the two planets with no moons at all; they have the least number of moons.
